abstract: 1. Phenotypic plasticity is an important mechanism by which organisms can cope with environmental change. However, there is growing recognition that phenotypic plasticity is not a single phenomenon but instead encompasses a range of responses that vary in reversibility and are predicted to evolve under different conditions. Nevertheless, few studies have disentangled the fitness effects and mechanisms of different forms of plasticity, making it difficult to predict their respective roles in promoting population persistence in the face of climate change. 2. In our study, we assessed plasticity of egg cold tolerance in the vector mosquito Aedes albopictus, considering both irreversible plasticity caused by photoperiodically-mediated diapause and reversible plasticity caused by cold acclimation. We also analyzed metabolites and lipids to investigate the extent to which these two forms of plasticity improve cold tolerance through shared mechanisms. 3. We found that diapause and cold acclimation independently enhance cold tolerance of Ae. albopictus eggs. While the beneficial effect of diapause on cold tolerance persisted throughout our experiment, cold tolerance gained through acclimation was lost when eggs were returned to warm temperatures. 4. Cold tolerance plasticity in Ae. albopictus does not appear to be driven by the accumulation of classical cryoprotectants. Instead, reductions in citric acid cycle intermediates and free fatty acids imply that diapause induces metabolic suppression, which likely helps maintain energy balance during winter and may also improve cold tolerance by protecting against cold-induced disruption of metabolic homeostasis. Cold acclimation generally increased lipid unsaturation, which may function to preserve membrane fluidity at low temperatures. Overall, diapause and cold acclimation imparted largely nonoverlapping effects on egg metabolite and lipid profiles, indicating that these two forms of plasticity act through distinct molecular pathways. 5. In addition to identifying potential mechanisms by which an invasive vector mosquito attains cold tolerance to survive winter, our results provide evidence that irreversible and reversible plasticity are distinct phenomena capable of evolving independently during populations' responses to novel environmental conditions.
